data.text:
#news #geopolitics #LamatinaleduBourdillon
---------------------------
1 Gaza
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sissi and US President Donald Trump will chair a ‘peace summit’ in Sharm el-Sheikh on Monday afternoon, attended by ‘leaders from more than 20 countries,’ including the French President and the British Prime Minister, Cairo announced on Saturday. The release of the remaining 20 Israeli hostages in exchange for 2,000 Palestinian prisoners is expected to take place shortly thereafter, but Hamas has announced that it will not participate in the signing ceremony, which does not bode well for the future, especially since it has announced that negotiations for the second phase of the American plan to end the war in Gaza will be ‘more complex’.
This phase provides for its disarmament and withdrawal from power, which it described on Saturday as ‘absurd’, as well as the deployment of an interposition force, mainly Turkish and Egyptian, to whom Canard Hirsute wishes good luck and thick bulletproof vests. Washington has begun deploying 200 military personnel to join their counterparts in the region responsible for this intervention. In areas of Gaza from which the Israeli army has begun to withdraw, Hamas has started arresting Palestinians it accuses of being collaborators and executing them without trial. https://t.co/pGCJrzw7i3
--------------
2 China-United States
Beijing accused the United States on Sunday of ‘double standards’ after Donald Trump announced additional 100% tariffs on Chinese goods, heralding a spectacular standoff that will soon be added to those already in force. ‘The US statement in question is a typical example of “double standards”,’ said a spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of Commerce in a statement posted online. Beijing fails to mention that Washington is responding to a crazy decision by China that the production and sale of any product containing more than 0.1% of its value in the form of ‘rare earths’ (about fifteen minerals essential to high technology, 90% of whose global production is located in China due to disregard for the environment) should be subject to approval by the Chinese authorities. Basically, Beijing wants to strictly control all trade in high-tech products worldwide. Shaggy Duck, for once, applauds Donald.
-----------------------
3 China/Philippines
On Sunday, the Philippine Coast Guard accused a Chinese vessel of ‘deliberately’ colliding with a Manila ship anchored near a disputed island in the South China Sea, in the Spratly archipelago, causing ‘minor damage’ with no injuries, while Beijing blamed the Philippines for being ‘entirely responsible’ for the collision. Sino-Philippine maritime incidents are very frequent in these waters, which China claims almost in their entirety despite an international ruling against it. We can expect that one day things will really escalate, particularly as Beijing tests Western reactions. More than 60% of global maritime trade passes through the South China Sea, which Beijing claims, sometimes so close to the coastline of neighbouring countries that even Shaggy Duck, who is not very good at gybing, could not go windsurfing there without provoking Beijing.
--------------------
4 Pakistan/Afghanistan
On Saturday evening, Taliban forces launched armed ‘retaliatory’ attacks against Pakistani soldiers along their shared border, accusing Islamabad of carrying out air strikes on their territory. On Friday, the Taliban Ministry of Defence blamed Pakistan for the explosions, accusing its neighbour of ‘violating its sovereignty’. Islamabad did not confirm that it was responsible, but called on Kabul ‘to stop harbouring Pakistani Taliban (TTP) on its soil’. The Pakistani government promised a ‘strong’ response on Sunday morning.
In recent months, TTP militants have intensified their campaign of violence against Pakistani security forces in the mountainous areas bordering Afghanistan. Islamabad believes that the Afghan Taliban, who returned to power in Kabul in the summer of 2021, are behind the resurgence of the TTP. Shaggy Duck chuckles, since it was Pakistan that supported and armed the Taliban in the past.
------------
5 Madagascar
Madagascan soldiers joined thousands of people demonstrating in the streets of the capital Antananarivo on Saturday, calling on the security forces to ‘refuse orders to fire’ on the population and condemning the recent police crackdown.
Saturday's demonstration in the capital of the large island, which is notable for being the only country in the world where the average per capita income has hardly increased since... independence in 1960, is one of the largest since the movement began on 25 September, starting as a protest against water and electricity cuts and mutating into a broader challenge to the political leaders in power, starting with President Andry Raojelina. The latter declared on Sunday that an ‘attempt to seize power illegally and by force’ was underway. He was installed in 2013 by a military coup, re-elected in 2018, then in 2023, in elections contested and boycotted by the opposition.
----------------- ------------
6 France
Weakened by the defection of LR, which will not participate in the government, aware that it is ultimately somewhat toxic to remain associated with an executive hated by 80% of French people, but will support it ‘text by text’ (basically the budget, at most, and that's it), Sébastien Lecornu faces the challenge of urgently putting together a government that may only last a few days (a record for brevity to be broken, by himself, at 2 p.m. last Monday).
Under the Constitution, Parliament must have 70 days to examine a draft budget before 31 December. The text would therefore have to be sent to Parliament on Monday or Tuesday, in principle after passing through the Council of Ministers, which cannot meet before Tuesday evening. We therefore risk having a draft budget that has been written by itself, only in France. Sébastien Lecornu, who resigned last Monday because ‘the conditions were no longer met’, promised on Saturday evening that he would do the same if they ‘were no longer met again’. The Prime Minister may also decide to appoint a small number of ministers with specific responsibilities, as well as the ministers of finance and the budget, in order to speed up the process.
The centrists of the UDI, who have a large group in the Senate, followed suit with the LR, while Emmanuel Macron's traditional ally, Horizons, Edouard Philippe's party, reserved its participation ‘pending what the Prime Minister will propose for the country’. Sébastien Lecornu is left with the presidential camp, which swallowed its criticism on Saturday, and François Bayrou's Modem party, which is ready to commit to his side, representing about one-fifth of MPs.
The entire left has called for the immediate censure of the Lecornu 2 government. So have the National Rally and Eric Ciotti's UDR. The Socialist group (69 MPs) remains the only one capable of saving the government, but has set the bar high. Without confirmation ‘of the abandonment of 49-3, measures to protect and strengthen the purchasing power of the French people and an immediate and complete suspension of the pension reform, we will censure it,’ the Socialist Party warned on Friday evening. Shaggy Duck can understand the desire to stop the futile struggle to save a Macronie that is clearly on its last legs, but doing so by pushing, as the PS is doing, the pay-as-you-go pension system into bankruptcy at the expense of young people seems to warrant a serious frown.
